title: What the Node Eats
passages:
The screen on reader two blinked green, then held. The figure at the reader did not move. One glove had tape wrapped across the knuckles, white and crinkled. No name came. No badge number was spoken, though the machine had just printed one: 2244.

Teodoro wiped his hands on a rag that was already too greasy to help. "Ivo's got two cartridges left," he said. "Six more cases on the 7-K if the line holds. You want the shop log, it's behind the cathode. You want Marlowe, he's on the couch. He can't walk yet."

The figure's voice was dry, like air leaking from a worn seal. "A claim can be acknowledged by any reader. A listed man is only released off the plate by his own receiving countersign. Those are the collection rules. You know them."

"I know them," Teodoro said. "I signed the plate myself. Marlowe's crew now."

The figure turned. The shop light caught the tape on the knuckles, nothing else. "Who patched the diaphragm with glove rubber?"

Teodoro opened his mouth, then closed it. Rhea stopped pumping. The bellows of the respirator hung halfway inflated, tethered to Ivo's face by a strap and hope.

"That's not your board," Teodoro said.

"The board doesn't answer questions. People do." The figure stepped back from reader two. "Ivo's diaphragm was patched with a disc of heavy glove rubber. I want the name."

"Rhea," Teodoro said. He looked at her. "Rhea patched it. Her brother. She's been hand-pumping him for two days."

Rhea did not look up from the rubber bulb in her hands. "And I've got one more cartridge after this one. Unless you're carrying spares in that coat, you can take your rules and go back up the ore stub where you came from."

The figure did not flinch. "The cartridges are on the 7-K. They'll arrive when the compressor priority trips. The question was who patched the diaphragm, not who's breathing because of it."

"That's Rhea too," Teodoro said. He was talking too fast, he knew it, but he could not stop. It was his flaw, and Marlowe would have said so if he were awake. Marlowe was awake enough to listen from the couch, eyes open, saying nothing.

The figure turned toward the shop door. "A listed man stays listed until he countersigns himself off. Marlowe knows that now. Tell him the reclamation unit does not care about his bunk."

Then the figure walked out into the ore stub, boots crunching on the gravel grade, and did not look back.

Rhea let the pump handle fall. "Who was that?"

Teodoro shook his head. "No name. No clearance. Just badge 2244 on a reader that does not issue badges."

"Two cartridges," Rhea said. She squeezed the bulb again, soft and mechanical. Ivo's chest rose. "Tell me that was enough."

Teodoro looked at reader two, where the green light was still holding. "He's gone up the ore stub. Nobody here can say how a stranger knew about glove rubber, or which brother was dying."

Rhea did not stop pumping. She kept her hand on the bulb, watching the door. "If someone was standing four feet from Marlowe's couch and knew about the patch, they've been inside this shop. They've been listening."

"Then they left," Teodoro said. He did not sound sure. "And they took their name with them."

The pump hall at Culvert Nine smelled of rust and old hydraulic fluid. A single kerosene lamp hung from a ceiling beam, throwing Brill's shadow long across the concrete. She stood with her arms folded, the light catching one side of her face and leaving the other in dark.

The eleven scrubber seals lay stacked on the floor where Kass and Ospina had carried them from the rig. V. Ospina's live authority ring sat seated in the reader cradle near the door, the cradle's light steady red — flagged for Kettering review, no sender behind it. Ospina turned the chipped crescent over in their palm instead, the die they had found in Kettering's tool void, not the authority itself.

Saul knelt at the chalk line, clipboard balanced on one knee, pencil hovering above the paper. They had not moved since the seals arrived.

Brill said, "You want the last five cases? You put Culvert Nine on Anza's board as a resupply stop. Listed. Named. Anyone with a reader can find us."

Kass said, "That's the point. A green chain needs a receiving node, not a hole in the wall."

Ospina looked at the red counter on the reader. "You get listed, you get resupply. You get resupply, your crew eats. You stay dark, you starve in the dark."

Saul said, "I can write it. Pencil only. Not ink. The board treats pencil as a proposal until a reader keys it live at Anza." They looked up at Brill. "And a green chain counts every case. The receiving jaw scans each scrubber canister against the manifest. You skim one canister for your own crew, the jaw sees a mismatch, and the whole chain faults. You can't take a single case off the top. Your people eat only if Anza's board stays clean."

Brill stared at them. The lamp light shifted as she breathed. "You're asking me to become a name anyone can read so your node doesn't miss a meal."

"We're asking you to trade like everyone else," Kass said. "You wanted a trade. Here it is."

Saul dragged the pencil down the clipboard. A thin gray line. C-U-L-V-E-R-T N-I-N-E. They held it there, the wood biting into their palm. "Resupply stop. Shift overlap. Receiving mark matches Bay 4 Shift 2. That's your price."

Brill uncrossed her arms. She stepped to the chalk line, took the pencil from Saul's frozen grip, and drew a hard mark through her own name underneath the station name. "Fine. But if my crew goes hungry because your board hiccups, I'm not the one who has to explain it to a reader."

She shoved the pencil back at Saul. The tip snapped off on the clipboard edge.

A sound came from the ore line outside the pump hall doors: not the steady hum of a ghost train, but the sharper, irregular clatter of a locomotive under power, moving too fast for a scheduled stop. Headlights cut through the cracked glass at the top of the doors, sweeping across the stacked scrubber cases.

Saul stood, clipboard tight against their chest. "That's not the 7-K schedule."

"Or it is, and it's early," Brill said. She did not move for the door. "Either way, the chalk is down. You want the cases, you'd better be ready to sign for them before whoever that is decides they don't need a stop."

The 7-K came up the ore line into Anza a few minutes past the shift bell, running hot and unscheduled, and stopped at the unlit siding because that was the only place the crew had left it a way in. Rhea heard it before she saw it — the clatter of a locomotive under power, not the smooth nothing of a ghost train. She did not take her hand off the bulb.

"Cartridges," Teodoro said, already at the door. "That'll be the cartridges."

"Then go get them," Rhea said. "I'm not leaving him to fetch my own air."

The respirator sat on the bench beside Ivo's cot, a squat gray box with a rubber bulb on a hose and a gauge on the front that Rhea had learned to read better than any person's face. The needle sat in the red. Ivo's chest rose when she squeezed and fell when she let go, and between squeezes the gauge told her the truth: the last cartridge was nearly spent, the wax-paper seal on the spare cut hours ago, the diaphragm she'd patched with a disc of heavy glove rubber flexing a little more each hour like it wanted to tear.

A loader Rhea didn't know came up from the siding with a case on a hand truck, cartridges packed in straw. Teodoro cut one loose and passed it to her.

"Cut it into the housing," Rhea said, "and don't breathe on it." She kept pumping with her left hand and worked the right. The wax paper came away in a curl. The cartridge went into the housing, and she seated it with her thumb until the collar clicked. The needle jumped, hesitated, and climbed out of the red.

The machine took the load. The bulb in her left hand went slack, not needed, and the bellows inside the box caught the cartridge pressure and started breathing for Ivo on their own.

Rhea took her hand off the pump.

She looked at it — her own hand, cramped into a claw from two days of squeezing — and flexed it open and shut, open and shut, like she'd forgotten what it was for. Ivo's chest rose. Fell. Rose. Nobody touched anything. Rhea stood over her brother with her empty hand shaking at her side.

"Don't," Teodoro said.

"I'm not crying," Rhea said. "It's the fluid in my eyes. Two days without sleep does that."

Then the shop lights steadied.

They'd been browning and swelling all night, dimming every time the compressor down the line drew a load. Now they came up full and stayed there, and under the bench the compressor relay closed with a solid clack Rhea felt in her teeth. A second needle on the respirator woke — the mains needle, the one fed off Anza's compressor instead of a cartridge — and pinned itself high and steady.

"Priority's back," Teodoro said. He was staring at the ceiling like it had insulted him. "Somebody filed for compressor priority. Whole shop's on the line now. He runs off Anza, not the cartridge. He's got the line."

Rhea looked at the gauge. She trusted that needle. She'd trust it over Teodoro, over a stranger with tape on his knuckles, over anybody's word. The needle said Ivo had all the air the compressor could push, long as Anza had power, and Anza had power.

"Fenn," she said.

"What?"

"Who else signs for priority at a reader. Fenn." She flexed her hand again. "He was down-line at Culvert Nine when it went green. Filed it there, from their reader, and didn't say a word to me. No trade. No 'sign Marlowe over.' Just put the power back."

Teodoro opened his mouth, and for once nothing came out of it.

"Course, I could be wrong," Rhea said. She sat on the edge of Ivo's cot, her hand finally still. "Could be the desk. Could be God in a hi-vis." She watched the mains needle hold. "Whoever it was can explain it at the desk. I'm not thanking a gauge."

"Whoever it was can explain it at the desk. I'm not thanking a gauge."

The voice from the couch was dry enough to strip paint. "Then don't thank me. I wasn't at Culvert Nine's reader."

Rhea turned. Marlowe was propped on one elbow, his splinted shoulder braced against the cushions, staring at the ceiling. He had been listening the whole time.

Teodoro wiped his hands on his rag. "You were at the desk, though. You signed the receiving jaw. You're on Anza's plate as living crew, countersigned and logged."

"That's the point," Marlowe said. "I signed on. Now I want to sign off."

Teodoro set the rag down. "The rule's the same one your visitor quoted at reader two. A claim can be acknowledged by any reader. A listed man is only released off the plate by his own receiving countersign. I can't turn that key for you, and nobody else can either."

Marlowe swung his legs over the side of the couch. His bare feet hit the concrete. "Then nobody's turning it. I stay listed."

"You don't have to," Teodoro said. "Fenn took Voss. The serve order's folded. The chain's green."

"Green doesn't mean clean," Marlowe said. "It means the printer ran. I'm still under claim. Badge 2244 just said so, four feet from where I'm lying. If I sign myself off now, I hand them a clean release. If I don't, they have to come take me off a node board that just ate, and they'll have to explain why."

Rhea flexed her empty hand. "You're volunteering to be their prisoner so the paperwork stays tidy?"

"I'm volunteering to be a listed man with a bunk instead of ballast with a lid," Marlowe said. He stood up, swayed, caught himself on the back of a chair. "Teodoro, put me on the board. Shop hand. Pump watch, seal check, sweeping grease—whatever you need. I'm listed anyway, so I might as well be useful while I'm stuck."

Teodoro looked at reader two. The green light still held, steady and dumb. "Shop hand," he said. "Bunk's the spare behind the cathode. Don't touch the compressor."

Marlowe nodded. He walked to the spare bunk, sat down, and said, "A bunk you can't leave is still better than a box you can't shout out of."

Reader two chimed. A slip of paper slid out, warm from the roller. Teodoro picked it up and read it once, then read it again. The claim line under Marlowe's name read: acknowledged, live, badge 2244.

The shop door opened. Headlights cut across the floor from the ore stub, sweeping past the respirator and stopping on Ivo's face. A vehicle idled outside, engine ticking as it cooled, and no one in the shop had called for a pickup.
